extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists) seeking literary agents / writers preparing first-page submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing the opening (first page) of a novel so agents will continue reading; focuses on common rejection causes on the first page and how to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion / Not enough detail about the protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Not enough detail about the protagonist to relate to him/her — reader doesn't know basic facts (gender, age), no clear protagonist on the first page; boring details; too passive/no action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear signposts about who the protagonist is and enough character detail to relate to them early. Avoid passive openings and ensure some purposeful action or clear perspective on page one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening with the weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning the page by describing the weather is a common, weak opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weather-based openings that offer little narrative or character information; start where story/action/character stakes are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not starting in the right place
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with mundane setup scenes (e.g., protagonist having breakfast) that aren't significant to the story's conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the manuscript at a scene or moment that matters to the plot or character arc — don’t include lead-in material that can be cut or moved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clunky internal dialogue / lack of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal narration that doesn’t have a distinct voice, reads as bland or generic, or is overly familiar/negative rhetoric (e.g., 'School sucks').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop an authentic, original narrative voice. Show rather than tell; avoid clichéd, flat internal comments. For YA, ensure voice has immediacy and fits the character's age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must sound authentic / YA voice needs immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue that does not sound true to the character’s age or world; YA protagonists must sound appropriate for their age (not younger) and convey immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make dialogue believable for the character and genre; ensure YA voices feel immediate and age-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overuse of italics / formatting gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive italics or other typographic emphasis that distracts the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics and emphasis sparingly; avoid formatting choices that interrupt readability or appear unprofessional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor typography / no white space / weird typeface / no indents
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript presentation problems that make text hard to read (lack of white space, unusual typeface, no paragraph indents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard manuscript formatting so the text is easy to read: readable font, proper indents, clear paragraphing and white space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overuse of adverbs / wordiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive adverbs and verbose phrasing that bloat prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tighten writing; prefer strong verbs and concise description. Edit for unnecessary modifiers and verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wandering verb tenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistent or shifting verb tenses within the opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent tense unless a deliberate and clear narrative reason exists to change it; check for accidental tense shifts in editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not edited for length
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript appears unedited or too long for its content; first page shows lack of pruning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit ruthlessly for length and focus, especially in openings — unnecessary material should be cut before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clunky writing / subject-object confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Awkward phrasing, sentence structure problems, archaic constructions (e.g., 'said he'), or general clunky prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish sentence-level craft so prose flows naturally; fix subject-object confusion and outdated/awkward constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetitive descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated descriptions or redundancies that make the opening feel tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetition; vary description and tighten to keep momentum on the first page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnecessary dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive or unneeded dialogue tags that clutter dialogue and slow pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple tags (said) or action beats and remove redundant tags that detract from voice and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present tense is risky / tricky
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of present tense can be problematic and is riskier to pull off effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using present tense, be aware it’s tricky and must be handled skillfully; consider whether past tense would better serve clarity and reader comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-length variety — avoid run-on breathy sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that are so long the reader would 'have to pause for breath' indicate a need for greater sentence-length variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length to improve rhythm and readability; shorter sentences can provide clarity and punch when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too info-dump-y
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive exposition or background delivered upfront (info-dumping) that stalls narrative and overwhelms readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy exposition on page one; reveal worldbuilding and backstory gradually through action and character choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too much sensory detail overshadowing character
rubrics_metrics.description: Overfocus on sensory description that prevents the reader from getting a sense of the protagonist’s character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance sensory detail with character insight — sensory detail should serve characterization or plot, not replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too many names introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing multiple character names early, making it unclear who is the main character to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit early-name introductions; prioritize clarity about who the reader should invest in on page one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pop-culture references can date the material/author
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy use of pop-culture references risks dating the book and the author, and may confuse readers unfamiliar with the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pop-culture references sparingly and carefully; ensure they won’t immediately age the manuscript or alienate some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologues are usually unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with a prologue is often not needed and can be a red flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider removing prologues unless they are essential and add immediate, unavoidable value for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening with an emotional breakdown before establishing stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with a protagonist's meltdown or emotional scene before the reader knows why they should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish investment in the character before dumping an intense emotional scene; give the reader reasons to care about the protagonist’s pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong religious beginning may be off-putting; focus on characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Very strong religious openings (e.g., a preacher’s rant) can throw off readers or oversimplify sides, especially in sensitive topics (e.g., religious LGBT fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with characters and avoid simplistic or caricatured portrayals of religious figures; if religion is central, present it in a way that doesn’t immediately alienate potential readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing fictional religions too closely on real ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a fictional religion that looks exactly like a real religion (example given: a fictional religion that was exactly like Islam) can be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drawing on real-world religions, change enough details to avoid apparent attacks or insensitive parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling your work 'literary' is risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Referring to your own work as 'literary' can suggest arrogance and may be used as an excuse not to edit for length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let others judge and label the work; focus on craft and editing rather than self-applying highbrow genre labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor is a positive advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents respond well to humor; making them laugh can be a plus in submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appropriate to your voice and story, well-executed humor can help make your opening stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter and strong premise matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents read the query letter first; a strong premise in the query can make them continue reading past a shaky opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a compelling query and premise to increase the chance an agent will persist through early weaknesses in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across first pages matters — recurring problems lead to rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same Page 1 problems persist across the first five pages, agents will likely issue a form rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the quality and standards shown on page one carry through the first several pages; fix systemic problems across the sample, not just page one.
